parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: conversion of a.c. to pulsating d.c.
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at Fig. 7.1 - you have an a.c. sine wave going in and four diodes arranged in a diamond around R. What do diodes allow to happen in only one direction?
Hint 2: Think about what happens to the negative half-cycles of the input. Are they blocked completely, or are they flipped over to become positive at the output?
parts.proper_answer: To provide full-wave rectification of the input voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Diode Bridge**
You are looking at four diodes in a bridge. Remember a diode conducts in the forward direction only, so the bridge cleverly steers current through R in the same direction on both halves of the input cycle.

Step 2: **Name the Process**
Changing alternating voltage into a unidirectional, pulsating direct voltage is called rectification. Because both the positive and negative half-cycles of $V_{IN}$ appear as positive pulses of $V_{OUT}$, as seen in Fig. 7.2, this is specifically full-wave rectification.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: Joule heating power P = V^2 / R
hints: Hint 1: Maximum power must happen at the moment of maximum voltage. Read the peak value of $V_{OUT}$ carefully from the top of the pulses in Fig. 7.2.
Hint 2: For a resistor, power is linked to voltage squared divided by resistance. Check which form of $P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R$ uses the $V$ and $R$ you know.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the Peak Voltage**
Power in a resistor grows with voltage squared, so the biggest $P$ is at the biggest $V$. From Fig. 7.2 the tops of all the $V_{OUT}$ pulses reach $$V_{max} = 9.0\text{ V}$$

Step 2: **Apply P = V^2 / R**
For Joule heating in resistance $R$: $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ At the peak: $$P_{max} = \frac{(9.0)^2}{370} = \frac{81}{370} \approx 0.219\text{ W} \approx 0.22\text{ W}$$ This is what was to be shown.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start from $P = V^2/R$. When $V_{OUT}$ is zero, what must $P$ be, and when $V_{OUT}$ is maximum, what must $P$ be?
Hint 2: Compare the time axis of Fig. 7.2 and Fig. 7.3. The zeros of power must line up with the zeros of voltage at 0, 0.02, 0.04 s and so on.
Hint 3: Think about the height of your curve. You have just calculated the top value in (b)(i), so what number on the $P$ axis should every hump touch?
parts.proper_answer: Sketch of rectified $V^2$ pulses: zero minima on time axis at 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08 s, same pulse rate as Fig. 7.2, with all peaks at 0.22 W.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Understand the Shape**
Since $$P = \frac{V_{OUT}^2}{R}$$ $P$ can never be negative. Where $V_{OUT}=0$, $P=0$, so the minima sit exactly on the time axis. Between zeros the curve rises smoothly like a squared sine wave, a little narrower and more peaked than the voltage humps.

Step 2: **Keep the Timing the Same**
Squaring does not create new zeros. So your $P$ pulses must have exactly the same period as the $V_{OUT}$ pulses in Fig. 7.2, with minima at $$t = 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08\text{ s}$$ and maxima halfway between, at about 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07 s.

Step 3: **Set the Peak Height**
From (b)(i) every voltage peak of $9.0\text{ V}$ gives $$P_{max} = 0.22\text{ W}$$ So draw all four humps touching $0.22\text{ W}$ on the $P$ axis of Fig. 7.3, starting at 0 and ending at 0.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
key_concepts: mean power of rectified sine wave
hints: Hint 1: For a sinusoidal-squared pulse train the average height over time is exactly half the peak height - how can you get the mean from your 0.22 W peak?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Halve the Peak**
For a sine wave, the time average of $\sin^2$ is $1/2$. So the mean heating effect is half the maximum: $$P_{mean} = \frac{P_{max}}{2} = \frac{0.22}{2} = 0.11\text{ W}$$

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Without the diodes, $V$ across R will now swing both positive and negative as a normal sine wave. But look at the power formula - does the sign of $V$ matter when you square it?
Hint 2: If the $P$ against $t$ graph ends up with exactly the same shape and area as before, what does that tell you about the average heating over time?
parts.proper_answer: The power-time graph is identical because $P = V^2/R$, so negative half-cycles give the same positive power. Hence mean power is equal to (b)(iii), 0.11 W.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Squaring Removes the Sign**
Heating power depends on $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ When R is straight across the a.c. supply, $V$ alternates positive and negative, but $(-V)^2 = (+V)^2$. So the negative half-cycles that were flipped up by the rectifier now still produce exactly the same positive power pulses.

Step 2: **Compare the Means**
That means the $P$ against $t$ graph is unchanged in shape, height and timing. Equal area under the $P$-$t$ graph means equal energy per second, so the mean power dissipated is the same as in (b)(iii).
